claim: Two alternative mechanisms for direction selectivity have been discussed in the literature: preferred direction enhancement and null direction suppression.
source: Two alternative mechanisms have been discussed in the literature so far: preferred direction enhancement, by which responses are amplified when stimuli move along the preferred direction of the cell, and null direction suppression, where one signal inhibits the response to the subsequent one when stimuli move along the opposite, i.e. null direction.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of motion detection, as indicated by the context of the introduction.

claim: Directional responses first appear in T4 and T5 cells along the processing chain in the Drosophila optic lobe.
source: Along the processing chain in the Drosophila optic lobe, directional responses first appear in T4 and T5 cells.
evidence: This is supported by prior research establishing T4 and T5 as the first direction-selective neurons.

claim: Both preferred direction enhancement and null direction suppression mechanisms are implemented in different sub-regions of the receptive field of T4 neurons.
source: Visually stimulating sequences of individual columns in the optic lobe with a telescope while recording from single T4 neurons, we find both mechanisms at work implemented in different sub-regions of the receptive field.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fly optic lobe consists of four consecutive layers of neuropil called lamina, medulla, lobula and lobula plate.
source: Photoreceptors send their axons into the optic lobe, which consists of four consecutive layers of neuropil called lamina, medulla, lobula and lobula plate (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about Drosophila visual system, also illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Each neuropil layer is made up of retinotopically organized columns containing roughly 100 different neurons per column.
source: Each neuropil layer is made up of retinotopically organized columns together containing roughly 100 different neurons per column (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989.

claim: Visual motion information is extracted in parallel pathways encoding light increments (ON) and decrements (OFF) within the optic lobe.
source: Within the optic lobe, visual motion information is extracted in parallel pathways encoding light increments (ON) and decrements (OFF) (Joesch et al., 2010; Eichner et al., 2011; Joesch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Both ON and OFF pathways bifurcate in the lamina and lead via specific medulla interneurons onto the dendrites of T4 and T5 cells, respectively.
source: Both pathways bifurcate in the lamina and lead, via a set of specific medulla interneurons, onto the dendrites of T4 and T5 cells, respectively (Takemura et al., 2013; Shinomiya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to connectomic studies.

claim: T4 and T5 cells exist in 4 subgroups tuned to one of the four cardinal directions of motion.
source: Both T4 and T5 cells exist in 4 subgroups tuned to one of the four cardinal directions of motion and project into four layers of the lobula plate (Maisak et al., 2013) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: T4 and T5 cells form monosynaptic cholinergic excitatory connections with the dendrites of the large-field lobula plate tangential cells.
source: There, they form monosynaptic cholinergic excitatory connections with the dendrites of the large-field lobula plate tangential cells (Mauss et al., 2014; Schnell et al., 2012) as well as with lobula plate intrinsic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Lobula plate intrinsic neurons inhibit tangential cells in the adjacent layer.
source: These intrinsic neurons, in turn, inhibit tangential cells in the adjacent layer (Mauss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mauss et al., 2015.

claim: None of the neurons upstream from T4 and T5 respond to visual motion in a direction-selective way.
source: Since none of the neurons upstream from T4 and T5 respond to visual motion in a direction-selective way (Behnia et al., 2014; Strother et al., 2014; Meier et al., 2014; Ammer et al., 2015; Serbe et al., 2016), T4 and T5 cells are the first neurons in the processing chain where directional information is represented explicitly (Maisak et al., 2013; Fisher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior functional studies.

claim: T4 and T5 cells are the first neurons in the processing chain where directional information is represented explicitly.
source: Since none of the neurons upstream from T4 and T5 respond to visual motion in a direction-selective way (Behnia et al., 2014; Strother et al., 2014; Meier et al., 2014; Ammer et al., 2015; Serbe et al., 2016), T4 and T5 cells are the first neurons in the processing chain where directional information is represented explicitly (Maisak et al., 2013; Fisher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations and follows logically from the previous claim.

claim: In preferred direction enhancement, the response to the sequence along the preferred direction is larger than the linear sum of responses to the isolated pulses.
source: in case of preferred direction enhancement, the response to the sequence along the preferred direction is larger than the linear sum of responses to the isolated pulses and identical if the sequence is along the null direction
evidence: This is a definition of the preferred direction enhancement mechanism based on established models.

claim: In null direction suppression, the response to the sequence along the preferred direction is identical to the linear sum of responses to the isolated pulses and smaller if the sequence is along the null direction.
source: In case of null direction suppression, the response to the sequence along the preferred direction is identical to the linear sum of responses to the isolated pulses and smaller if the sequence is along the null direction.
evidence: This is a definition of the null direction suppression mechanism based on established models.

claim: Individual T4 and T5 neurons extend their dendrites across multiple columns.
source: Individual T4 and T5 neurons extend their dendrites across multiple columns (Figure 1e) and receive synaptic inputs from different medulla cell types located in different columns relative to the home columns of the T4 or T5 neuron and to each other (Takemura et al., 2013; Shinomiya et al.; 2014).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1e showing T4 dendrite morphology and citations to connectomic studies.

claim: T4 and T5 neurons receive synaptic inputs from different medulla cell types located in different columns.
source: Individual T4 and T5 neurons extend their dendrites across multiple columns (Figure 1e) and receive synaptic inputs from different medulla cell types located in different columns relative to the home columns of the T4 or T5 neuron and to each other (Takemura et al., 2013; Shinomiya et al.; 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to connectomic studies.

claim: The optical system and neuronal wiring in flies obeys the neural superposition principle.
source: The structure of the optical system and of the neuronal wiring in flies obeys the neural superposition principle (Kirschfeld, 1967; Braitenberg, 1967).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Photoreceptors R1-6 from 6 neighboring ommatidia that share the same optical axis converge on the same lamina cartridge, forming an optical column.
source: Those photoreceptors R1-6 from 6 neighboring ommatidia that share the same optical axis converge on the same lamina cartridge, thus forming an optical column that represents the unit of spatial resolution ('neuro-ommatidium').
evidence: This is established knowledge about the neural superposition principle in fly vision.

claim: L2 cells responded maximally to stimuli at a certain column, with less than 30% response amplitude to stimuli positioned on surrounding columns.
source: L2 cells responded maximally to stimuli at a certain column, with less than 30% response amplitude to stimuli positioned on surrounding columns, and negligible responses (<12%) to stimuli positioned on columns in the next outer ring (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is experimental data from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2a.

claim: L2 cells showed negligible responses (<12%) to stimuli positioned on columns in the next outer ring.
source: L2 cells responded maximally to stimuli at a certain column, with less than 30% response amplitude to stimuli positioned on surrounding columns, and negligible responses (<12%) to stimuli positioned on columns in the next outer ring (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is experimental data from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The slight activation of neighboring columns results directly from the optics of the fly's eye, where visual fields of single ommatidia have Gaussian sensitivity profiles with an acceptance angle roughly matching the inter-ommatidial separation.
source: The slight activation of neighboring columns results directly from the optics of the fly's eye, where the visual fields of single ommatidia have Gaussian sensitivity profiles with an acceptance angle roughly matching the inter-ommatidial separation (Götz, 1965).
evidence: This is an inference based on known optical properties of the fly eye, supported by citation.

claim: T4 cells have a larger receptive field than L2 cells, with about 50% amplitude to stimuli onto the six surrounding columns.
source: Compared to L2, however, the receptive field was found to be larger, with about 50% amplitude to the stimuli onto the six surrounding columns, and roughly 25% to the next outer ring (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is experimental data from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2b.

claim: T4 cells showed roughly 25% response amplitude to stimuli in the next outer ring of columns.
source: Compared to L2, however, the receptive field was found to be larger, with about 50% amplitude to the stimuli onto the six surrounding columns, and roughly 25% to the next outer ring (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is experimental data from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2b.

claim: T4 neurons pool excitatory synaptic input from more than one column.
source: This indicates that T4 neurons pool excitatory synaptic input from more than one column, consistent with their morphology (Figure 1e) and expected from a motion detector that is required to integrate information from spatially offset input.
evidence: This is inferred from the receptive field data and consistent with morphological observations.

claim: When T4 cells were stimulated sequentially from ventral to dorsal, the cell responded more strongly than expected from the sum of the responses to the individual stimuli.
source: When stimulated sequentially from ventral to dorsal (Figure 3a, 'Sequence', top middle), the cell responded more strongly (thick blue line) than expected from the sum of the responses to the individual stimuli (thin blue line).
evidence: This is experimental data from apparent motion experiments shown in Figure 3a.

claim: When T4 cells were stimulated sequentially from dorsal to ventral, the cell responded more weakly than expected from the sum of the responses to the individual stimuli.
source: The opposite was observed when we stimulated the cell sequentially from dorsal to ventral (Figure 3a, 'Sequence', bottom middle): now the cell responded more weakly (thick red line) than expected from the sum of the responses to the individual stimuli (thin red line).
evidence: This is experimental data from apparent motion experiments shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Both preferred direction enhancement and null direction suppression contribute to the directionally selective responses of T4 cells.
source: We then calculated the nonlinear response component by subtracting the linear expectation from the actual response and found that both preferred direction enhancement (Figure 3a, 'Sequence', top right) and null direction suppression (Figure 3a, 'Sequence', bottom right) contributes to the directionally selective responses of T4 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Preferred direction enhancement is shifted towards the 'null-side' and null direction suppression towards the 'preferred side' with respect to each other in the receptive field.
source: We conclude that the different mechanisms are offset in their receptive fields: preferred direction enhancement is shifted towards the 'null-side', and null direction suppression towards the 'preferred side' with respect to each other.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 3b showing spatial segregation of mechanisms.

claim: When pulses were placed onto the ventral part of the receptive field with the upper pulse delayed with respect to the lower one (PD), responses peaked at a delay of about 500 ms.
source: When we placed the pulses onto the ventral part of the receptive field, delaying the upper with respect to the lower one (PD), responses peaked at a delay of about 500 ms (Figure 3c, top).
evidence: This is experimental data from temporal delay experiments shown in Figure 3c.

claim: When pulses were placed onto the dorsal part of the receptive field with the lower pulse delayed with respect to the upper one (ND), responses were suppressed and returned to baseline at a delay larger than 500 ms.
source: When the pulses were placed onto the dorsal part of the receptive field, delaying the lower with respect to the upper one (ND), responses were suppressed and returned to base line at a delay larger than 500 ms (Figure 3c, bottom).
evidence: This is experimental data from temporal delay experiments shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Null direction suppression builds up over longer sequences of steps.
source: We also noticed that this null direction suppression builds up over longer sequences of steps (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: When the stimulation of the central column was preceded by stimulation of one directly adjacent column on the 'preferred side', the response to the central pulse was strongly suppressed.
source: When the stimulation of the central column was preceded by the stimulation of one directly adjacent column on the 'preferred side', the response to the central pulse was strongly suppressed as before (red trace).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The suppression from null-direction sequences can lead to a response that falls below the flicker response to the central column, indicating inhibition.
source: This suppression led to a response to the sequence that on average not only falls below the sum of both individual stimulations, but even below the flicker response to the central column (black trace), indicating inhibition.
evidence: This is experimental data and interpretation shown in Figure 3d.

claim: When a null-direction sequence was extended from two to three columns, the resulting response was even smaller.
source: When this null-direction sequence was extended from two to three columns, the resulting response was even smaller (green trace).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: For zero onset time differences (simultaneous stimulation of two columns), the response was suppressed compared to stimulation of just one column.
source: The experiments shown in Figure 3c also revealed that for zero onset time differences, i.e. simultaneous stimulation of two columns, the response was suppressed as compared to stimulation of just one column.
evidence: This is experimental data from Figure 3c.

claim: The response in T4 neurons was suppressed for simultaneous stimulation of the central column together with another one in the dorsal part of the receptive field.
source: The resulting response in the T4 neuron was found to be suppressed in comparison to the isolated central column response for simultaneous stimulation of the central column together with another one in the dorsal part of the receptive field.
evidence: This is experimental data from the systematic receptive field mapping shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Using large horizontal bars (180° × 4.5°), flicker responses of T4 cells were almost undetectable.
source: Using a bar size of 180° × 4.5°, indeed, flicker responses of T4 cells were almost undetectable (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: With large bars, apparent motion stimuli along the preferred direction led to pronounced responses larger than the linear prediction, while null direction sequences did not suppress the negligible sum of flicker responses by a significant amount.
source: Apparent motion stimuli along the preferred direction led to pronounced responses, larger than the linear prediction, while null direction sequences did not suppress the negligible sum of flicker responses by a significant amount (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Using small bars (4.5° × 3°), strong flicker responses appeared in T4 cells.
source: This was much different when repeating the same stimuli using bars of only 4.5° × 3° instead: now, as in the experiments employing telescopic stimulation of individual columns, strong flicker responses appeared (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: With small bars, in addition to preferred direction enhancement, pronounced null direction suppression was observed with peak sensitivity within the dorsal part of the receptive field.
source: Furthermore, in addition to the preferred direction enhancement, pronounced null direction suppression was observed with peak sensitivity within the dorsal part of the receptive field (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The model combining preferred direction enhancement and null direction suppression exhibits a high degree of directional selectivity over a broad range of velocities, with little responses to null direction motion.
source: We found that the model exhibits a high degree of directional selectivity over a broad range of velocities, with little responses to null direction motion (Figure 5c, middle left).
evidence: This is data from computational modeling shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The model without null direction suppression revealed substantial null direction responses almost as large as its preferred direction responses.
source: In contrast, the model without null direction suppression revealed substantial null direction responses almost as large as its preferred direction responses (Figure 5c, middle center).
evidence: This is data from computational modeling shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The model without preferred direction enhancement revealed substantial null direction responses almost as large as its preferred direction responses.
source: The same was true for a model with no preferred direction enhancement (Figure 5c, middle right).
evidence: This is data from computational modeling shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The full model T4 cell is more sharply tuned to its preferred direction than the one without preferred direction enhancement or the one without null direction suppression.
source: When we simulated the responses of the model to grating motion into different directions, we found the full model T4 cell to be more sharply tuned to its preferred direction than the one without preferred direction enhancement or the one without null direction suppression (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is data from computational modeling shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Combining preferred direction enhancement with null direction suppression leads to a strong direction selectivity of the primary motion-sensing unit.
source: We conclude that combining preferred direction enhancement with null direction suppression leads to a strong direction selectivity of the primary motion-sensing unit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Over a wide range of velocities spanning more than two orders of magnitude, T4/T5 cells responded almost exclusively to upward motion along their preferred direction, with little or no responses to motion along their null direction.
source: Over a wide range of velocities spanning more than two orders of magnitude, T4/T5 cells responded almost exclusively to upward motion, i.e. along their preferred direction, with little or no responses at all to motion along their null direction (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is experimental data from calcium imaging with moving gratings shown in Figure 6a.

claim: When stimulated with 1 Hz grating motion at various directions, T4/T5 cells showed a rather sharp directional tuning with about 90° half-width around its preferred direction.
source: When stimulating the cells with 1 Hz grating motion at various directions, we found a rather sharp directional tuning with about 90° half-width around its preferred direction (Figure 6b; see also Figure 3g in Maisak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 6b and supported by prior work.

claim: T4/T5 cells with blocked synaptic output revealed the same high degree of directional selectivity as control cells.
source: T4/T5 cells revealed the same high degree of directional selectivity as before (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is experimental data from tetanus toxin block experiments shown in Figure 6c,d.

claim: The mechanism underlying the high degree of directional selectivity in T4 cells does not include the output of oppositely tuned T4 cells but rather originates in the dendrite of the cells.
source: From this, we conclude that the mechanism underlying the high degree of directional selectivity in T4 cells does not include the output of oppositely tuned T4 cells but rather originates in the dendrite of the cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tetanus toxin block experiments.

claim: The Hassenstein-Reichardt model leads to weakly direction-selective signals in the first place, which are improved downstream by subtraction of oppositely tuned components.
source: In the Hassenstein-Reichardt model (Hassenstein and Reichardt, 1956) as well as in the Barlow-Levick model (Barlow and Levick, 1965) direction selectivity emerges by a nonlinear interaction of asymmetrically filtered signals from adjacent image points: an enhancement along the preferred direction in the first, and a suppression along the null direction in the second model. Both models lead to weakly direction-selective signals in the first place, which, in the Hassenstein-Reichardt model, are improved downstream by subtraction of oppositely tuned components (for review, see Borst and Helmstaedter, 2015.
evidence: This is established knowledge about motion detection models, supported by citations.

claim: A high degree of directional selectivity is found already at the first stage where directional responses are observed, i.e. in T4 and T5 cells.
source: Surprisingly, however, a high degree of directional selectivity is found already at the first stage where directional responses are observed, i.e. in T4 and T5 cells (Maisak et al., 2013) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Improving the direction-tuning already at the level of the half-detectors by additional null-direction suppression increases robustness to noise and might be energetically less costly.
source: Improving the direction-tuning already at the level of the half-detectors by the additional null-direction suppression increases robustness to noise and might in addition be energetically less costly.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional advantages of the mechanism.

claim: The findings require that T4 cells receive input from more than two cell types.
source: In contrast to the cellular implementation of the motion detector proposed by Behnia et al, 2014 our findings also require that T4 cells receive input from more than two cell types.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The requirement for more than two input cell types is in agreement with recent connectomic data.
source: This again is in agreement with recent connectomic data (for T4 cells: Louis Scheffer, Janelia Research Campus, personal communication; for T5 cells: Shinomiya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by connectomic data from personal communication and citation.

claim: Functional studies where synaptic input elements onto T4 and T5 neurons were blocked suggested the involvement of more than two input elements in the ON- and OFF-pathways.
source: Finally, functional studies where the synaptic input elements onto T4 and T5 neurons were blocked also suggested the involvement of more than two input elements in the ON- (Ammer et al., 2015) as well as in the OFF-pathway (Serbe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The inputs representing the enhancing, direct and suppressing input segregate on different sub-regions of the T4 dendrite, with enhancing inputs on the 'null-side' and suppressing inputs on the 'preferred side' of the dendrite.
source: Considering the columnar nature of the input elements and the structure of the T4 dendrites covering multiple columns, we predict, that the inputs representing the enhancing, direct and suppressing input segregate on different sub-regions of the T4 dendrite, with enhancing inputs on the 'null-side' and the suppressing inputs on the 'preferred side' of the dendrite.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings and anatomical considerations.

claim: The visual fields of single ommatidia have Gaussian sensitivity profiles.
source: The slight activation of neighboring columns results directly from the optics of the fly's eye, where the visual fields of single ommatidia have Gaussian sensitivity profiles with an acceptance angle roughly matching the inter-ommatidial separation (Götz, 1965).
evidence: This is established knowledge about fly optics, supported by citation.

claim: The acceptance angle of single ommatidia roughly matches the inter-ommatidial separation.
source: The slight activation of neighboring columns results directly from the optics of the fly's eye, where the visual fields of single ommatidia have Gaussian sensitivity profiles with an acceptance angle roughly matching the inter-ommatidial separation (Götz, 1965).
evidence: This is established knowledge about fly optics, supported by citation.

claim: Flies see the world through a hexagonal array of facets each equipped with its own small lens focusing light onto 8 photoreceptors.
source: Flies see the world through a hexagonal array of facets each equipped with its own small lens focusing the light onto 8 photoreceptors.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about fly visual system.

claim: The relatively small differences between large, but poorly tuned signals in the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator would be highly prone to noise.
source: While the output of the full Hassenstein-Reichardt-correlator after the subtraction stage shows a high degree of directional selectivity in the absence of null-direction suppression, the relatively small differences between large, but poorly tuned signals (see Figure 5c, middle panel) would be highly prone to noise.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results shown in Figure 5c.

claim: A recent study concluded preferred direction enhancement as the sole mechanism underlying elementary motion detectors in Drosophila.
source: A recent study addressing the mechanisms underlying the elementary motion detectors in Drosophila concluded preferred direction enhancement as the sole mechanism (Fisher et al. 2015).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: The stimulation paradigm used by Fisher et al. 2015 consisting of flashes at 2 positions simultaneously does not allow discrimination between different mechanisms including lateral inhibition, adaptation and null direction suppression.
source: However, we find that their stimulation paradigm consisting of flashes at 2 positions simultaneously does not allow to discriminate between different mechanisms including lateral inhibition, adaptation and null direction suppression.
evidence: This is a critical inference about the limitations of prior work.
